summary: US-015: Channel allocations — caps and scheduled release
description:
### US-015: Channel allocations — caps and scheduled release
**As** an organizer, **I want** to split a slot's sellable capacity across sales channels with
per-channel caps and scheduled give-back, so presales and resellers can't starve the public
on-sale. **Priority:** P1 **Depends on:** US-014 (extends the same claim-model surface; soft —
parallelizable if Planning confirms no schema overlap)
**Acceptance Criteria:**
- [ ] A pool can carry channel allocations (opaque channel code + cap + optional release-at
      time); allocations never sum above pool capacity; unallocated capacity is the default/public
      channel.
- [ ] Holds carry a channel; a hold beyond its channel's remaining allocation is rejected even
      when the pool has capacity (and vice-versa: pool exhaustion rejects regardless of channel
      headroom). The no-oversell proof extends to per-channel caps under the contention test.
- [ ] At `release-at`, a channel's unsold allocation returns to the public channel — enforced by
      DB time like TTL expiry (lazy, correct without a sweeper); the release is observable in
      availability reads.
- [ ] Channel codes are opaque strings here; the channel registry, per-channel pricing and
      windows stay in TKT-17/TKT-5 (non-goal).

**Quality gates (every story):**
- `make check` green (lint + unit + integration + smoke; mirrors CI)
- Contract tests pass for any touched service boundary (ADR-009 drift check)
- Money/ticket-path: audit-trail invariants hold (ADR-003)
- Read-endpoint changes: ADR-004 TTL tier declared with rationale

Parent epic: TKT-4. Full lineage: docs/product/prd-v1.md §TKT-4.

objective.note: Epic COS 3: split sellable capacity across channels with caps and scheduled give-back so presales/resellers can't starve the public.

scope.note: IN: allocations (opaque code + cap + release-at) on a pool, channel on holds, dual rejection (channel cap / pool capacity), lazy scheduled release. OUT: channel registry, per-channel pricing/windows (TKT-17/TKT-5).

uncertainties.note: Sub-pool rows vs cap counters is the main design fork — Planning decides against the lock-order rules.

dependencies.note: Soft on US-014 (same claim-model surface); parallelizable if Planning confirms no schema overlap — not wired as a blocker.

approach.note: Allocation table keyed to pool; channel column on claims joins the availability math under the existing pool lock; contention test extends to per-channel caps.

first_slice.note: Allocate 100 of a 1000 pool to 'presale' with release-at T; presale hold 101 rejects; after T the unsold 100 are publicly claimable.

success.note: The 4 ACs + quality gates; per-channel no-oversell under contention is the load-bearing signal.

binding.rule: The inventory database is the sole write-side correctness boundary. Each mutation locks the inventory pool row first, then its claim rows; operations addressed by hold ID discover the pool with a non-locking read, then re-read the claim after locking the pool — every path has the same pool-to-claim lock order. A claim is held, confirmed, released, or expired; the last three are terminal. PostgreSQL time decides expiry: a transaction expires due holds before capacity accounting, so cleanup jobs are optional optimizations. Confirmed plus unexpired-held quantity may never exceed pool capacity. Hold creation requires an organizer-scoped idempotency key, single-use across the claim's full lifecycle. Reserved seats, date ranges, and entitlements reuse the lifecycle and lock ordering but add their own resource constraints.

governingAdrs.why: Channel caps are a second accounting dimension inside the same pool lock — lazy DB-time release mirrors hold expiry (sweep before accounting, no sweeper needed for correctness).
Allocation config + channel on holds change the OpenAPI contract and possibly the hold request fingerprint — idempotency replay semantics must stay exact.
